lines.text: Human connections take many forms, each with its own vocabulary. Romantic relationships progress through stages: two people might start as acquaintances, become friends, and then begin dating. A boyfriend and girlfriend may become engaged — a fiancé and fiancée — before becoming a married couple: husband and wife, or simply spouses. Not all relationships are smooth. Couples sometimes argue, separate, or even divorce, becoming ex-partners. Some choose to remain single, while others prefer cohabiting — living together without marrying. Beyond romance, social roles define how we interact. A colleague is someone you work with, while a classmate shares your classes. A neighbour lives near you, and a flatmate or roommate shares your home. A mentor guides and advises, while a mentee learns from their experience. In families, roles like guardian, caretaker, and godparent carry specific responsibilities. A best friend is your closest companion, an ally supports you, and a rival competes with you. Understanding these relationship terms helps navigate social situations, fill out official forms, and discuss personal life with precision and confidence.

lines.text: In modern English, 'partner' is widely used instead of 'boyfriend/girlfriend', especially for long-term relationships or when being gender-neutral. It's considered more mature and inclusive. 'Significant other' and 'other half' are also common.

lines.text: In English-speaking cultures, a proposal often involves a ring. The engagement period involves wedding planning, choosing a best man and bridesmaids, and sending invitations. 'Engaged' is always followed by 'to', never 'with'.

lines.text: 'Flatmate' is British English; 'roommate' is American English. Both mean someone who shares your living space. In American English, 'roommate' can mean sharing a flat (not necessarily the same room), which confuses some learners.
